I have always loved the hour just after rain, when streets turn into mirrors and the city seems briefly forgiven for its noise. At that moment, every pavement holds a private sky: clouds, pale light, the occasional passing face, all trembling slightly beneath my feet. People walk faster, yet I imagine they slow. A bicycle bell rings from somewhere unseen, sharp and bright, and pigeons rise from a ledge in a disorderly gray explosion.

Rain has a way of editing the world. It softens brick walls, blurs windows, and erases the sharp edges between things. Trees become darker versions of themselves. Cars glide past with shining flanks. Even the air smells changed—clean, mineral, almost metallic—and I breathe deeper without deciding to.

I like walking without a destination during this weather. A forgotten bookstore appears, its window crowded with faded letters. A café radiates warmth and the smell of coffee. Under an awning, someone smiles as if sharing a secret. I do not enter either place. I simply carry them onward, two small offerings against the gray.

Sometimes rain is merely weather, and I should stop pretending it is a philosophy. Still, I welcome those intermissions when the world washes itself and reveals, briefly, how much beauty it had all along.

Tonight, if clouds return, I will leave my umbrella behind. Let rain tap my shoulders, cool my hands, and blur lampposts into halos. I will meet no one and discover that solitude can feel like companionship whenever the world listens.
